chapters.title: Chapter 1: Your First Java Program
chapters.goal: Build a simple application using an IDE and AI tooling and learn the syntax of Java that makes your program run.

examples.title: Hello World
examples.description: Write a simple Hello World program in Java.
examples.prompt: Write a Hello World program in Java.

explanation.summary: This is the traditional first Java program: it prints the single line "Hello, World!" to the screen and then ends. Everything else in the file is the minimum structure Java requires before you are allowed to run one statement.

lines.text: Every Java statement lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name exactly, so this code has to be saved as HelloWorld.java. Getting this pair out of step is the most common first error a beginner meets.

This is the entry point: when you run the program, Java looks for a method with precisely this signature and starts there. The words are not decoration, and changing any of them means Java can no longer find where to begin.

System.out is the standard output stream (your console) and println writes the text followed by a newline. The text in double quotes is a string literal, printed exactly as typed, and the semicolon ends the statement.

Braces come in pairs and close in the reverse order they were opened: this last one closes the class, after the inner braces have closed main. Indentation is only for human readers, but keeping it tidy is how you spot a missing brace.

replay.prompt: Write a Hello World program in Java.
commentary: This is the traditional first Java program: it prints the single line "Hello, World!" to the screen and then ends. Everything else in the file is the minimum structure Java requires before you are allowed to run one statement.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Dynamic Programming with Variables and Input
chapters.goal: Generate an application that you can interact with and learn how variables act as the memory of software programs.

examples.title: Variable Declaration
examples.description: Declare variables in Java to remember values for later.
examples.prompt: Create a reminder by declaring a String variable and print the reminder.
response: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";

explanation.summary: This program stores a reminder message in a variable and then prints that variable to the console. It is the first step beyond printing text directly: the text now lives in a named container that can be reused and changed in one place.

lines.text: The class name must match the file name exactly, so this code belongs in a file called DisplayReminder.java.

lines.code: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";
lines.text: Java requires you to state the type of data a variable holds, so the declaration begins with String, the type used for text. The name reminder is the label you use to refer to that text later, and the value in double quotes is what gets stored in it.
Notice there are no quotation marks here: passing reminder without quotes tells Java to look up the value stored in the variable, whereas "reminder" would print the word itself.

replay.prompt: Create a reminder by declaring a String variable and print the reminder.
commentary: This program stores a reminder message in a variable and then prints that variable to the console. It is the first step beyond printing text directly: the text now lives in a named container that can be reused and changed in one place.

examples.title: Print Number
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a number variable.

prompts.prompt: Write code that prints a number variable.

explanation.summary: This program stores the number 42 in a variable and prints it to the console. It is the same shape as the reminder example, but the variable holds a number instead of text.

lines.text: The type comes first: `int` tells Java this variable holds a whole number, so the value 42 is stored as a number rather than as text. Try changing 42 to your own favorite number and running the program again.
There are no quotation marks around `number`, so Java prints the value stored in the variable rather than the word "number". Wrapping it in quotes is the most common beginner slip here.

replay.prompt: Write code that prints a number variable.
commentary: This program stores the number 42 in a variable and prints it to the console. It is the same shape as the reminder example, but the variable holds a number instead of text.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add two numbers and display their sum.

explanation.summary: This program stores two whole numbers in variables, adds them together into a third variable, and prints the result. It is the previous PrintNumber example extended to perform a mathematical operation.

lines.text: A variable declaration names a piece of memory and gives it a value; `int` means it holds a whole number, so `a` can be used later anywhere the value 20 would work.

The AI might have picked different numbers, or added them directly inside `println` and skipped the `sum` variable entirely. Variations like these are fine as long as the code is clear and the result is the same.
The `+` operator adds the two values, and the result is stored in a new variable named `sum`. Naming the result makes the intent of the calculation obvious to anyone reading the code.
Passing the variable rather than a number prints whatever `sum` currently holds, so changing the values of `a` and `b` changes the output without touching this line.

replay.prompt: Update the code to add two numbers and display their sum.
commentary: This program stores two whole numbers in variables, adds them together into a third variable, and prints the result. It is the previous PrintNumber example extended to perform a mathematical operation.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Short and Int
examples.description: Explore the differences between short and int data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a short data type and an int data type.
response: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short

explanation.summary: This program stores one whole number in a short variable and a larger one in an int, then shows what happens when the two are used together in arithmetic. It prints both values along with their sum and the doubled short.

lines.text: A short reserves only 16 bits, so it holds whole numbers from -32,768 to 32,767 — enough for 12,345 but nowhere near a million. The underscores in the literal are purely for readability; Java ignores them, so 12_345 and 12345 are the same number.
An int uses 32 bits and comfortably holds a million, which is why it is the everyday choice for whole numbers when memory is not tight.

lines.code: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
lines.text: Java automatically widens the short to an int before adding, because moving to a larger type cannot lose any part of the value. This is implicit widening casting, and you never have to ask for it.

lines.code: short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short
lines.text: Multiplying a short produces an int result, so storing it back into a short is a narrowing conversion that Java refuses to do on its own. The (short) in front is you taking responsibility for the fit — and since 24,690 is under 32,767, nothing is lost here.
The + between a string and a number is concatenation, not addition: Java converts shortValue to text and joins it onto the label.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using both a short data type and an int data type.
commentary: This program stores one whole number in a short variable and a larger one in an int, then shows what happens when the two are used together in arithmetic. It prints both values along with their sum and the doubled short.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Widening Type Casting
examples.description: Explore widening type casting in Java by converting integer variables to double in a calculation.
examples.prompt: Write code to calculate splitting the length of a piece of printer paper into 2 pieces, converting two integer variables to a double in the calculation.
response: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)

explanation.summary: This program divides an 11-inch sheet of printer paper into 2 equal pieces and prints the length of each piece. Because the two measurements are stored as whole numbers, they are widened to double so the division keeps its fractional part.

lines.code: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)
lines.text: The paper's length is a whole number of inches, so int is the natural type to hold it. The comment records where the value came from, which is exactly what comments are for.

The (double) in front of each value is the widening cast: it promotes each int to a decimal type before the division happens, so the result is 5.5 rather than 5. Without the casts Java would divide integer by integer, throw away the remainder, and quietly give the wrong answer.
The + here joins text to a number: Java converts eachPieceLength to its printable form and glues the three parts into one line of output.

replay.prompt: Write code to calculate splitting the length of a piece of printer paper into 2 pieces, converting two integer variables to a double in the calculation.
commentary: This program divides an 11-inch sheet of printer paper into 2 equal pieces and prints the length of each piece. Because the two measurements are stored as whole numbers, they are widened to double so the division keeps its fractional part.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Narrow Type Casting
examples.description: Explore narrowing type casting in Java by converting a double variable to an int.
examples.prompt: Write code to narrow casting by displaying an integer value of a price of $100.30 for an advertisement.
response: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int

explanation.summary: This program stores a price with cents in a double and then converts it to an int, dropping the decimal part so an advertisement can show a round dollar amount. It prints $100 instead of $100.30.

lines.text: The real selling price needs a type that holds decimals, so it goes in a double.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: The (int) written in front of price is an explicit cast: because an int cannot hold decimals, Java requires you to state the target type as a way of confirming you accept the loss.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: Narrowing truncates rather than rounds, so 100.30 becomes 100 — and 100.99 would also become 100, not 101.
Joining the number to a string with + turns it into text for display, which is why the dollar sign can sit right next to the value.

replay.prompt: Write code to narrow casting by displaying an integer value of a price of $100.30 for an advertisement.
commentary: This program stores a price with cents in a double and then converts it to an int, dropping the decimal part so an advertisement can show a round dollar amount. It prints $100 instead of $100.30.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Float and Double
examples.description: Explore the differences between float and double data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a float data type and a double data type.
response: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float

explanation.summary: This program stores the value of pi in two decimal types \  64-bit double, prints both, then adds them and converts the double back down to a float. It shows how Java handles decimal numbers of different sizes and what happens when you squeeze the larger one into the smaller one.

lines.text: The trailing f is required: Java treats every decimal literal as a double by default, so without it the compiler refuses to put 3.14 into a float variable.
A double has room for roughly twice as many significant digits, which is why it is the usual choice for calculations where precision loss matters.

lines.code: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
lines.text: When a float and a double are added, Java widens the float to a double automatically and the result is a double \ no cast needed, because nothing can be lost going up in size.

lines.code: float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float
lines.text: Going the other direction discards digits, so Java makes you write the cast to confirm you accept the loss.
Compare this line's output with the printed double: the tail of pi is simply gone, which is narrowing precision loss you can see.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using both a float data type and a double data type.
commentary: This program stores the value of pi in two decimal types \  64-bit double, prints both, then adds them and converts the double back down to a float. It shows how Java handles decimal numbers of different sizes and what happens when you squeeze the larger one into the smaller one.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Boolean
examples.description: Explore the boolean data type in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without using logic like an if statement.
response: // Combine booleans with logical operators (no if/switch/?:)

explanation.summary: This program shows Java's boolean type, which holds only true or false. It creates booleans directly, derives them from number comparisons, and combines them with logical operators, printing each result.

lines.text: A boolean variable has exactly two possible values, true and false, written as bare keywords with no quotation marks.

A comparison is itself an expression that produces a boolean, so the result of == can be stored in a variable rather than tested immediately. Note that == compares values while a single = assigns, which is a common slip.
The ! operator flips a boolean to its opposite and && produces true only when both sides are true, so this variable means that not everything passed but something did.
Several conditions can be chained with && to form a single yes-or-no answer; because allPassed is false here, readyToSubmit is false no matter what the other two say.
Joining a boolean to a string with + converts it automatically to the text true or false, which is how the program reports its results without any if statement.

examples.title: Pizza Party Calculator
examples.description: Create a pizza calculator in Java that calculates the number of pizzas needed based on the number of people in a party and slices per pizza.
examples.prompt: Write a simple pizza calculator with variables for people in party and slices per pizza.

explanation.summary: This program figures out how many pizzas to order for a party by storing the party size, the slices in each pizza, and how many slices each person will eat, then doing the arithmetic and printing all the values back out.

lines.text: All three starting values are whole numbers held in int variables, which is the right choice here because you cannot invite half a person or order a fraction of a pizza. Change any of these three and run the program again to see the order recalculated.
A variable can hold the result of a calculation, not just a value you type in, and that result then becomes an ingredient in the next calculation.

Dividing two ints in Java throws away any remainder, so 20 slices divided by 8 would give 2 pizzas and leave four people hungry. Adding one less than a full pizza before dividing rounds the answer up, which is how a real order works.

The plus sign between text in quotes and a variable joins them into one message rather than adding numbers; Java converts the number to text for you. Printing the inputs alongside the answer lets the customer confirm the order is based on the right assumptions.

replay.prompt: Write a simple pizza calculator with variables for people in party and slices per pizza.
commentary: This program figures out how many pizzas to order for a party by storing the party size, the slices in each pizza, and how many slices each person will eat, then doing the arithmetic and printing all the values back out.

examples.title: Welcome {Name}
examples.description: Write a Welcome {Name} program in Java using a variable to store the name.
examples.prompt: Write a Welcome {Name} application without taking input.

explanation.summary: This short program stores a person's name in a variable and joins it onto a greeting so the message prints as one line of text. It is the starting point for a welcome application, before any user input is involved.

lines.text: The name lives in a regular local variable, not a final constant, so the host can swap in whichever guest is arriving and run the program again.
The + here is string concatenation: the literal text and the variable's value are assembled into a single string before printing, the way you would paste cut-out words together to form a note.
Notice the space inside the quotes after "Welcome". Concatenation adds nothing of its own, so leaving that space out would print "WelcomeAda".

replay.prompt: Write a Welcome {Name} application without taking input.
commentary: This short program stores a person's name in a variable and joins it onto a greeting so the message prints as one line of text. It is the starting point for a welcome application, before any user input is involved.

examples.title: Welcome {Name} with Input
examples.description: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that takes the user's name as input.
examples.prompt: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that accepts the user's name as input.

explanation.summary: This program asks the user to type their name, reads what they type from the console, and prints a personalized welcome message.

lines.text: A Scanner is the tool Java uses to read input, and passing System.in tells it to read from the console where the user is typing. The full package name java.util.Scanner is spelled out because the class lives in Java's utility package; exercise 2-12 shows the shorter form using an import.
Using print instead of println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the user types their name right after the prompt rather than on the line below.
nextLine reads everything the user typed up to the Enter key and stores it in the name variable, which is what makes the welcome sign dynamic rather than hard-coded.
The + here joins the fixed text to the value the user supplied. Note the space inside the quotes after "Welcome" \u2014 without it the output would read "WelcomeAva".
Closing the Scanner releases the input resource when the program is finished with it, a habit worth forming for anything you open.

replay.prompt: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that accepts the user's name as input.
commentary: This program asks the user to type their name, reads what they type from the console, and prints a personalized welcome message.

examples.title: Calculate cake servings with division and modulus operators
examples.prompt: Create an intro Java example for serving 2 cake slices per person using mathematical operators for division and modulus.
response: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division

explanation.summary: This program works out how many people a cake will serve when each guest gets two slices, and how many slices are left over. It uses the division operator to get the number of guests and the modulus operator to get the remainder.

lines.text: Starting with 23 slices and a portion size of 2 gives a division that does not come out even, which is exactly what makes the leftover interesting.

lines.code: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division
lines.text: Because both operands are int, Java performs integer division and throws away any fraction, so 23 / 2 is 11 rather than 11.5 — and that is the honest answer here, since half a portion does not fully serve anyone.
The modulus operator returns what division discarded, which is the single slice left for the guest of honor to take home.
Names like peopleFullyServed and slicesPerPerson attach meaning to the numbers, so the calculation reads like the question it answers instead of a bare 23 / 2.

replay.prompt: Create an intro Java example for serving 2 cake slices per person using mathematical operators for division and modulus.
commentary: This program works out how many people a cake will serve when each guest gets two slices, and how many slices are left over. It uses the division operator to get the number of guests and the modulus operator to get the remainder.

examples.title: Import statement instead of full package name for Scanner
examples.prompt: Rewrite this code to use an import statement for Scanner rather than the full package within the code.

explanation.summary: This program asks the user to type their name at the console and then greets them by name. It is the same program as before, except the Scanner class is brought in with an import statement at the top instead of being spelled out with its full package name inside the code.

lines.text: The import tells Java once, at the top of the file, that "Scanner" means the Scanner class in the java.util package. This is the alternative to writing java.util.Scanner everywhere the class is used, and it is what you ask the AI for when it generates the full package name inline.
Because of the import, the class needs only its short name here. The Scanner is attached to System.in, the console, so it reads whatever the user types.
print is used rather than println so the cursor stays on the same line, letting the user type their answer right after the prompt.
nextLine() waits for the user to press Enter and hands back the whole line as text, which is stored in the name variable for later use.
Closing the Scanner releases the console input so the program is not left waiting for more typing, freeing it up for whatever comes next.

replay.prompt: Rewrite this code to use an import statement for Scanner rather than the full package within the code.
commentary: This program asks the user to type their name at the console and then greets them by name. It is the same program as before, except the Scanner class is brought in with an import statement at the top instead of being spelled out with its full package name inside the code.

examples.title: Example showing boolean data type
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without conditional logic.

explanation.summary: This program declares two boolean variables, prints their values, and then combines them with logical operators to work out a third value. It shows that a boolean can only ever hold true or false, and that Java can calculate one boolean from others.

lines.text: A boolean variable stores one of exactly two values, true or false. Notice that true is a Java keyword, not the text "true" in quotes, so no quotation marks belong here.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java converts it to the word true or false for display, which is why the output reads as plain English.

This is the logical part: ! flips hasBugs from false to true, and && demands that both sides be true before the whole expression is true. The value is computed from the other two variables rather than typed in by hand.
The result is true here because Java is fun and there are no bugs; change either starting variable and this line reports a different answer, which is the decision tree in action.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without conditional logic.
commentary: This program declares two boolean variables, prints their values, and then combines them with logical operators to work out a third value. It shows that a boolean can only ever hold true or false, and that Java can calculate one boolean from others.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Controlling Code with Conditions and Loops
chapters.goal: Learn how to apply control structures in order to build more advanced applications that make use of logic and iteration.

examples.title: If Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a game's level if a condition is met.

prompts.prompt: Write a Java program without input that prints 'Novice Level' if the number variable is less than 10.

explanation.summary: This program stores a player's game level in a variable and prints "Novice Level" only when that level is below 10. It is the simplest form of a decision in Java: one condition, one outcome.

lines.text: The player's current level is held in a variable so the decision below can be made about whatever value happens to be there. Change this to 15 and the program prints nothing at all.

The condition to evaluate goes inside the parentheses after the if keyword, and the less-than operator asks whether the level falls under the novice threshold. Thresholds like this are one of the most common kinds of condition you will write, whether for discounts, alerts, or game levels.

Everything inside the braces runs only when the condition is true, which is why this line is indented one level further than the if. Without a matching else clause, a level of 10 or higher produces no message whatsoever.

replay.prompt: Write a Java program without input that prints 'Novice Level' if the number variable is less than 10.
commentary: This program stores a player's game level in a variable and prints "Novice Level" only when that level is below 10. It is the simplest form of a decision in Java: one condition, one outcome.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add an else to print 'Expert Level' and update the variable to fit that criterion.

explanation.summary: This program stores a player's level in a variable and prints one of two messages depending on whether that level is below 10. The `else` block guarantees the player always sees a status, even when the `if` condition is not met.

lines.text: The value stored here decides which branch runs, and 12 was chosen so the condition fails — that is how you see the `else` block do its job.
The condition in the parentheses is a question with a yes-or-no answer; the block that follows runs only when the answer is yes.
The `else` clause is the "otherwise" plan, covering every value that the condition rejected. There is no condition to write here because it handles all remaining cases.
Because 12 is not less than 10, this is the line that actually prints. Exactly one of the two blocks runs — never both, and never neither.

replay.prompt: Update the code to add an else to print 'Expert Level' and update the variable to fit that criterion.
commentary: This program stores a player's level in a variable and prints one of two messages depending on whether that level is below 10. The `else` block guarantees the player always sees a status, even when the `if` condition is not met.

prompts.prompt: Add an else if for an 'Intermediate Level'.

explanation.summary: This program checks a player's level number against a cascade of conditions and prints the matching skill tier. With the number set to 12, it prints "Intermediate Level".

lines.text: The player's level is fixed here so you can see the middle branch fire; change it to 5 or 25 and rerun to watch a different tier print.
The first condition is tested first, and only if it fails does Java move on to the next clause. Order matters, because the cascade stops at the first match.
The else-if adds a second criterion to check before falling through to the default. Note that it does not need to say "10 or more": reaching this line already means the first condition was false.
The else is the default plan for when none of the conditions match, so exactly one of these three messages always prints.

replay.prompt: Add an else if for an 'Intermediate Level'.
commentary: This program checks a player's level number against a cascade of conditions and prints the matching skill tier. With the number set to 12, it prints "Intermediate Level".

examples.title: Ternary Operator
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses a ternary operator to print a game level.
examples.prompt: Use a ternary operator to print a game level as novice, intermediate, or expert based on a number variable.
response: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test

explanation.summary: This program picks a game level name from a number using the ternary operator, a compact one-expression alternative to an if/else chain, and prints the result.

lines.code: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test
lines.text: The single number that drives the whole decision; edit it and re-run to see each branch fire in turn.
A ternary is an expression that produces a value, so it can sit directly on the right of an assignment: the condition before the ? is tested, and the value after it is used when the test is true.

The part after the colon is the "otherwise" value, and here it is another ternary. Chaining this way is how a ternary handles more than two outcomes, and because we only reach it when levelNumber is not below 10, the test needs no lower bound.
Every ternary must supply a final else value, so this last branch has no condition and catches anything 20 or above. The semicolon ends the assignment statement that began three lines earlier.
The decision was already made when level was assigned, so printing is a separate, trivial step; keeping the choice and the output apart lets you reuse level elsewhere.

examples.title: Switch/Case Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays the status of a process based on a number variable.
examples.prompt: Use a switch statement to evaluate a status number variable and print 'Starting' for 1, 'Processing' for 2, 'Ready' for 3, and 'Unknown' as default.

explanation.summary: This program tracks a coffee shop order by checking a status number and printing the matching message. A switch statement compares the value of status against each case and runs the block that matches, or the default block when nothing matches.

lines.text: This is the single value the switch will evaluate. Change it to 1, 3, or something like 9 and rerun to see each branch, including the default, take over.
The switch takes one expression and compares it against each case label in turn, which is tidier than a long chain of else-if tests when you are matching a variable against fixed values.
Without break, execution falls through into the following case blocks and prints their messages too. The break exits the switch immediately, so only the matching status message appears.
The default block is the backup for any value that no case matched, such as an unknown or errored order. It is last, so it needs no break.

replay.prompt: Use a switch statement to evaluate a status number variable and print 'Starting' for 1, 'Processing' for 2, 'Ready' for 3, and 'Unknown' as default.
commentary: This program tracks a coffee shop order by checking a status number and printing the matching message. A switch statement compares the value of status against each case and runs the block that matches, or the default block when nothing matches.

examples.title: While/Do-While Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses while and do-while loops to print numbers.

prompts.prompt: Write a coffee order program using a while loop to print the status and increment until it reaches 100.

explanation.summary: This program tracks a coffee order's progress with a while loop, printing the status in ten percent steps until it passes one hundred, then announcing that the coffee is ready.

lines.text: The counter has to exist and hold a starting value before the loop runs, because the loop's condition is checked against it on the very first pass.

This condition is tested before every repetition, so the body runs only while the status has not yet passed one hundred. Using <= rather than < is what lets the loop print the "100%" line before it exits.

This is the line that eventually makes the condition false. Leave it out, or put it after the closing brace, and status stays at zero forever, giving you an infinite loop that eats resources and never finishes.
Because this sits outside the loop's braces, it runs exactly once, after the loop has dropped out at status 110.

replay.prompt: Write a coffee order program using a while loop to print the status and increment until it reaches 100.
commentary: This program tracks a coffee order's progress with a while loop, printing the status in ten percent steps until it passes one hundred, then announcing that the coffee is ready.

prompts.prompt: Change the code to use a do-while loop instead of a while loop.

explanation.summary: This program counts a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100% in steps of ten, printing each status update, then announces that the coffee is ready. It uses a do-while loop, so the status message is guaranteed to appear at least once.

lines.text: The do keyword marks the start of the block, and there is no condition here at all — the body runs before anything is evaluated, which is exactly what you want when the customer must be informed at least once.
Something inside the body has to move status toward the stopping point, otherwise the condition would stay true forever and the loop would never end.

The condition now sits at the end and is checked after each pass, so the loop repeats while the status has not yet passed 100. Note the semicolon: a do-while statement requires one here, unlike an ordinary while loop.
This line is outside the loop, so it runs once after the condition finally fails and the loop is done.

replay.prompt: Change the code to use a do-while loop instead of a while loop.
commentary: This program counts a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100% in steps of ten, printing each status update, then announces that the coffee is ready. It uses a do-while loop, so the status message is guaranteed to appear at least once.

examples.title: For Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that loops through numbers or items in a list and prints each one.

prompts.prompt: Use a for loop to increment a lap number variable and print each lap.

explanation.summary: This program uses a for loop to run three laps around a track, printing each lap number, then prints a message once the loop finishes.

lines.text: All three parts of the loop's control live in the parentheses, separated by semicolons: the counter starts at 1, the loop keeps going while lap is 3 or less, and lap grows by one after each pass. Because the number of iterations is known up front, there is no need to check anything by hand the way a while loop would.
Starting at 1 and using <= 3 gives laps 1, 2, and 3. Beginners often mix these up and write < 3, which stops after two laps, or start at 0 and print a "Lap 0" nobody ran.
This is the body that repeats, and it can use lap because the counter is in scope inside the loop. The + joins the text with the current number, so each pass prints a different line.
This line sits outside the closing brace of the loop, so it runs once after the condition finally fails. Indentation alone does not decide that — the braces do.

replay.prompt: Use a for loop to increment a lap number variable and print each lap.

explanation.summary: This version of the farmers' market app runs the "organic summer items sorted by price" pipeline across multiple threads instead of one. The only change from the earlier version is the method that starts the stream.

lines.text: The book has collapsed the product setup into comments below this line, so the list stays empty and the program prints an empty result; add a few MarketProduct objects here to see real output.

This single word is the whole change. Where stream() processes items one at a time in a single lane, parallelStream() splits the list across several threads, processes the chunks simultaneously, and merges the results.
Filtering is a stateless operation: each product is judged on its own values, with no reference to its neighbors, which is exactly what makes it safe to run in parallel.

Sorting is stateful, since the order of any one item depends on all the others. Java still gets it right in parallel by sorting each chunk and merging, but that merge is extra work and is where the overhead of parallelism shows up on small lists.

The pipeline never mutates a MarketProduct or the original list; it builds a brand-new list of names, so there is no shared state for threads to corrupt. That, plus the immutability of MarketProduct, is the answer to the thread safety question.
